claims.text: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has excellent mechanical properties at room and elevated temperatures.
The proposed intervention replaces Ta completely with an equimolar amount of Nb, producing HfMoNbTiZr.
Replacing Ta with Nb will decrease the alloy density.
The density decrease resulting from Ta-to-Nb substitution is expected to be 5–10%.
HfMoNbTiZr will retain the high room-temperature strength of HfMoTaTiZr.
HfMoNbTiZr will retain the high strength of HfMoTaTiZr at approximately 1000 °C.
HfMoNbTiZr will have minimal, if any, degradation in creep resistance relative to HfMoTaTiZr near 1000 °C.
Ta-to-Nb substitution will retain a similar refractory BCC or related solid-solution microstructure.
The substituted alloy will retain lattice distortion and precipitation behavior comparable to the baseline alloy.
Nb has a density of approximately 8.57 g/cm³, whereas Ta has a density of approximately 16.65 g/cm³.
Nb can play a role similar to Ta in stabilizing a high-entropy refractory solid solution.
Lowering the contribution from heavy elements is the mechanism by which Ta-to-Nb substitution reduces overall alloy density.
Atomic-scale lattice interactions and dislocation impediments underpin strength retention at room temperature and near 1000 °C.
The proposed performance boundary is static tensile or compressive loading from room temperature through approximately 1000 °C.
The comparison applies to alloys produced using similar conventional casting and homogenization routes.
The effects of Nb substitution on density and mechanical properties depend on phase stability, microstructural evolution, and atomic interactions.
The hypothesis is rejected if density decreases by less than 3% or if yield strength or creep resistance decreases by more than 10% relative to the baseline.

contradictions.description: The baseline is repeatedly described as as-cast, while the comparison is also described as using casting and homogenization. A homogenized specimen is no longer strictly in the as-cast state, so the intended processing state of the control is internally ambiguous.
